title: Anthropic launches Claude Ship, agents review, fix, & approve code changes now
content:
Anthropic is moving from having Claude write code to helping developers decide when that code is ready to ship. On Monday, the newly public AI company announced the launch of Claude Ship, a suite of AI agents for automating code reviews, fixes, and approvals of routine code changes.
The latter is the more interesting part of this new set of tools, as AI coding tools already offered code review features before now. What’s notable about Claude Ship is not just that it can review proposed code changes and identify and address problems, but that it also includes an agent that can approve code changes automatically based on policies set by a development team.
The launch arrives at a time when AI coding agents have become increasingly capable of generating substantial amounts of code, leading to bottlenecks in reviewing and approving the code changes before they go live. With Claude Ship, the idea is to automate even more of the work involved in the development process, essentially by delegating approval authority to an AI agent itself.
“Most teams want a person to approve every change, and that’s easy to keep up with when people write every line. But a lot of developers build with agents now,” a company blog post explains. “On the Claude Code team, Claude writes most of our code, and we wanted everything after the PR to move that fast too.”
Claude Ship is launching in beta, allowing early adopters to use it to review pull requests (PRs), and then decide what’s ready to merge.
The new offering consists of Code Review, which is already generally available, and two new agents now in beta: PR Steward and Claude Approvals. PR Steward focuses on addressing issues such as failing CI checks, merge conflicts, and feedback from Code Review. It also comments after every push on what it changed and how to roll it back, if needed.
Claude Approvals then applies an approval policy that the team writes as a file in the repository. This approval process can incorporate various signals, including Code Review findings or the company’s own classifiers, with policies written in natural language.
Because the offering is still in beta, Anthropic suggests running the approval functionality in observe-only mode first. Teams can also choose to start with just one repository and set monthly spending limits to have more control over the process.
Anthropic says teams will also still remain in control of where Claude Ship runs, which review settings to use (e.g., Quick, Standard, or Deep), and which changes should be escalated to a human for a decision.
Claude Ship is rolling out to Claude Team and Enterprise plans for repositories on GitHub. Code Review is generally available, while PR Steward and Claude Approvals are in beta.

report.summary: Anthropic's Claude Ship adds AI agents that review pull requests, fix CI failures and merge conflicts, and auto-approve routine changes under team-written policies, in beta on GitHub.
report.background: AI coding agents have become good enough that many teams now generate far more code than humans can comfortably review. That creates a new bottleneck: pull requests pile up, CI checks fail, merge conflicts accumulate, and senior engineers spend their time on routine sign-off rather than architecture. Anthropic says its own Claude Code team already has Claude writing most of its code, and wanted everything after the PR to move at the same speed. Meanwhile, AI code review tools like CodeRabbit and Greptile are already common, so differentiation has shifted from "can it spot a bug" to "can it decide what ships." Claude Ship is Anthropic's answer: a bundle that pushes the agent past commenting on diffs and into the approval step itself, turning team policy into an executable file in the repository. It also fits Anthropic's broader push toward agentic products after becoming a public company.
key_points: Claude Ship bundles three pieces: Code Review, which is already generally available and flags problems in proposed changes; PR Steward, in beta, which actively fixes failing CI checks, merge conflicts and Code Review feedback, then comments after each push on what it changed and how to roll it back; and Claude Approvals, also in beta, which decides whether a change can merge.

The genuinely new part is Claude Approvals. Teams write an approval policy as a file inside the repository, in natural language, and the agent applies it using signals like Code Review findings and Anthropic's own classifiers. That effectively delegates merge authority to a model, rather than just using AI as an advisory reviewer.

The motivation is throughput, not novelty. As agents generate large volumes of code, human review becomes the slowest step in the pipeline. Anthropic frames Ship as extending automation from writing code to deciding when code is ready to ship, matching how its own internal team already works.

Anthropic has built in guardrails for the beta: run approvals in observe-only mode first, start with a single repository, set monthly spending limits, choose review depth (Quick, Standard or Deep), and define which changes must escalate to a human for a final call.

Distribution is limited for now. Claude Ship is rolling out to Claude Team and Enterprise plans for repositories hosted on GitHub, with Code Review generally available and the two new agents in beta, so it is aimed at organizations rather than individual hobbyists.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the notable shift is that agents are crossing from suggestion into authorization. Auto-approval turns model judgement into a governance question, and it will push competitors like GitHub, GitLab and code review startups to offer policy-driven agent gatekeeping rather than just diff comments. For developers, the job shifts toward writing and auditing approval policies, tuning review depth and handling escalations, while routine merge chores get absorbed by agents. That raises real questions about accountability when a model approves a flawed change. For regular users, the likely effect is faster shipping and more frequent updates, with a corresponding risk that subtler bugs slip through when nobody reads the diff. Expect enterprises to demand audit trails and conservative observe-only rollouts before trusting automatic merges.
report.tools: To follow up, look at Claude Code and Claude Ship (Team/Enterprise, GitHub), plus the beta docs on policy files. Comparable review agents include CodeRabbit, Greptile and Graphite. For open-source building blocks, try OpenHands and SWE-agent for autonomous issue-and-PR work, Aider for agentic editing in the terminal, Danger JS and reviewdog for rule-based PR gatekeeping, and Open Policy Agent if you want to express merge policy as code rather than natural language.
